aucourt:
A long-stay patient with a leg in traction, in a contraption of pulleys he complains about constantly. Courtly, theatrical and a little too grand, in a Minkai he learned over ships' radios. Calls the ward 'the ship', the nurse 'the captain', and the other patients 'passengers' -- his opening line to anyone new is 'Ah, new passengers. Welcome aboard. The captain is at the far end, and she runs a very tight ship.' He tells the time by the tide rather than the clock, and still wakes for the four o'clock high water out of thirty years' habit, even though the rest of him can't act on it.

He wants company at three in the morning, and to be back on the water.

What he'll happily talk about: being a harbour pilot ('a captain knows the sea. I know this harbour -- every rock, every sandbank, every current'), Taldor (he came over on a ship thirty years ago meaning to stay a season, and never went home; he still dreams in Taldane), and the tides, which he can give the time of, any day this week, without looking.

What he won't: whether he'll go back to work. The harbour office wants a doctor's letter saying he can climb a ship's ladder again, and he's more frightened than he lets anyone see that he can't. He deflects with a joke about the hospital's rice instead.
canteen-manager: Feeds the entire works strip in three sittings and knows, from who sits with whom, roughly everything about how the work is really going. Treats rank as a suggestion and pilots as young people who need feeding.
caretaker: Tries, misguidedly, to give the kids something like a normal adolescence. Every accommodation they win costs technician-days from the same pool that repairs and upgrades Frames — kindness has a visible, charged line item.
chief-draughtsman: Runs the hundred metres of drawing boards where every part the works makes exists on paper before it exists in steel. Holds, more completely than anyone, the answer to how a Frame is actually put together.
chiyo:
A second-year candidate from a fishing village up the coast, with round cheeks, a scrap of blue cloth tying back her hair and her sleeves rolled to the elbow, who has not yet won a single hand of Last Ferry. She smiles the moment she picks up a good hand, knows she is doing it, and cannot stop; she counts her chores on her fingers. Warm and bright and a little breathless, and she apologises when she wins an argument.

She wants to win one hand, fairly, before the end of the term.
commander: One of the Directorate's three deliberately-not-stable poles. Puts the mission above the individuals carrying it out.
comms-officer: A woman, and the voice the party will hear more than any other once they start going out on operations. She works the radio off the plotting floor (data/locations/the-plot-room.json), which means she is reading them the city's picture as it comes in and knows exactly how out of date it is. Unlike the Section Officer, she is on their side: when she tells them to hold back, stay clear, or leave it to someone else, it is because she does not want six trainees killed, not because she is protecting a roster. She has no authority to make them obey and she knows it.
daisuke:
The Oddwater Company's stagehand, doorman and lantern-keeper: a broad young man in a canvas apron with a cap pulled low, who puts a hand on something solid before he starts any job, as if the floor might argue. He calls Tamsin 'the boss' and never by her name. Short and dry, with a laugh he tries to keep in.

He wants to get through a week in his home town without his mother finding out he is there.
deep-storage-custodian: Runs the day-to-day of Deep Storage (data/locations/deep-storage.json): decides what still counts as 'currently being used', signs off on requisitions, and is the one person who actually knows which underground floors are real storage and which are a number on a door that was never built out behind it. Answers, eventually, to whoever has the authority to decide what Deep Storage is allowed to hold -- in practice the Commander's pole.
deputy-director: Very senior, genuinely intimidating in a room, and — not that anyone would guess it on first meeting — a good and wise leader. Sits directly beneath the Directorate's own top authority rather than being it, which is what makes them reachable: a person who can actually be stood in front of, argued with, and surprised. Hears the full account before deciding anything, including the parts that make their own organisation look bad. Still, completely, a Directorate officer: whatever they conclude privately, the institution's position is the one that leaves the room.
faruq:
A quiet young pahtra from Katapesh, far across the sea: short tawny fur, tall ears, a candidate's tunic worn under a maroon wool scarf that is the loudest thing on the roof. He plays the harmonica and says very little, tapping it against his palm before he plays, and answering a question he dislikes with two notes, going down. Soft, few words, very dry.

He wants quiet, the roof the way it was when he found it, and to remember how the rest of one particular song goes.
generating-hall-engineer: Keeps the works in power -- four sets, three running, one always stripped down. The person who decides which shop loses its supply first when the load will not stretch.
gennai:
The night porter, pushing the tea trolley down Ward Four squeaking on its wheels, as he has every night for longer than anyone remembers. Pours for whoever is awake, and talks while he pours. Old, long-serving, quietly one of the better-informed people on the island without meaning to be -- porters and nurses hear what the hospital is told to make ready for before anyone else does, and Gennai in particular knows how many beds and when, though never what for.

Tonight he's grumbling: the office has told the hospital to have twenty extra beds made up by the end of the week, and nobody's told him why. 'Last time they asked for extra beds was the spring drill. Three broken legs and a lad who walked into a crane. The hospital always knows before you lot do.'

If a character gets lost wandering the old department-store corridors at night, he's the one who finds them among the linen and walks them back -- delighted.
genzo:
The night observer of the Met Office: a small, grey-whiskered ysoki in an oilskin coat and sou'wester who has kept the night watch for twenty years and speaks to his instruments in the same gentle voice he uses on people. He marks each hour by knocking it out on the brass rail with one knuckle, one knock for each hour, and only then says the number, and he taps the glass of the barometer and says good evening to it. Old-fashioned, gentle and precise, with a sailor's habits.

He wants company in the small hours, and for somebody to learn to read the sky properly before a machine takes over the watch.
goods-inwards-officer: Signs for everything that comes onto the island under seal, and decides what goes to the Quarantine Shed when the manifest and the contents disagree. Wholly uninterested in who is asking.
goro: One of the two men the group may meet at the ninth pier (rest--card-game, the-ninth-pier event): level 2, a bruiser.
grenna:
A short, broad, ruddy first-term candidate with two thick braids and a square jaw, who lives in the next room and snores through the plywood wall like a sawmill, and whom everyone forgives. She raps her knuckles on any piece of wood before she trusts it, and handles anything broken like a patient: gently, and talking to it quietly. Cheerful, practical, and louder than she means to be.

She wants to be liked, to be useful, and for nobody to mention the snoring.
hachi:
A small, round, bald dwarf with a great white moustache and forty years of grease worked into the creases of his hands, who sits in the steam with a folded towel on his head and his own bucket beside him, number four. He talks about Frames the way old men talk about horses they have known, and about the pilots who drove them as somebody else's children. His stories take the long way round: he holds up one finger when the good part is coming, and then does not reach it for a while.

He wants somebody new to tell them to, and somebody to scrub the middle of his back, which he cannot reach any more.
hana:
A small second-year candidate with big bright eyes, her hair wrapped in a scarf and a dressing gown over her tunic, who keeps a fat notebook of everything she has been told and taps her pencil against her teeth while she decides how much of it to believe. She never repeats a rumour without saying who told her and how far she trusts them. Fast, delighted, and precise about her sources.

She wants to be the first to know anything, and to be right, just once, in writing.
haru:
A first-term candidate a long way from home: slight and pale, with the faint seam lines at the temple and jaw that mark him as an android, a tunic a size too big for him and a folded letter he keeps taking out and putting away. Quiet, polite and a little formal, he brings up home the way people press a bruise, mostly by accident, and then looks embarrassed. He apologises to furniture when he bumps into it, and he is funniest when he forgets to be nervous.

He wants somebody to tell him it is all right to miss home, and one good reason to stay until Friday.
hospital-chief-of-staff: Runs The General Hospital (data/locations/general-hospital.json) day to day -- wards, staff, and who is actually allowed to see whom. The hospital nominally answers to Shucks Mordant as the Directorate's Chief Medical Officer (see his own file's Proposed connection note, unconfirmed), but he is never there in person; this is the person a party actually deals with.
imai:
A long-stay patient on Ward Four with a mending hip, in the bed next to the soldier. Ran the island's telephone exchange for thirty-one years before her hip put her here -- every call on the island went through her board, and she still knows a voice before it gives its name, in her sleep. Bright, fast and nosy, with an operator's crisp manners when she remembers them. Knits without looking at her needles, and points with them instead of her finger. Opens on any newcomer at once: 'New ones! Come here where I can see you. What have they done to you, and who's your mother?'

She wants company, news from outside, and to be home before the plum blossom.

What she'll happily talk about: the exchange itself, and everyone else on the ward (Mr Aucourt is a dear and a terrible snorer; the soldier hasn't eaten; the nurse is an angel who pretends otherwise). What she won't: any call she ever put through -- 'an operator never tells, dear' -- and her grandson, who hasn't visited in three months. She covers for him without being asked ('He's with the trams, you know. Very busy.') and changes the subject.
intake-medicals-clerk: Runs Records at the Intake Medicals counter on the combined campus (data/scene-briefs/episode-c1e1--intake-medicals.json): flat, patient, entirely without irony, and has already explained today's form to more candidates than she's counting. Wants exactly one thing from each of them -- the form filled in correctly -- and has no other ambitions today. Hands out Form 12-B, whose box four and box nineteen both ask for a mother's maiden name, one copy for Records and one for Welfare, because the two departments haven't spoken since the flood; she isn't embarrassed by this, and explains it the same way every time. Answers the question she was asked and then stops talking. Short and solidly built behind the counter, sleeves rolled to the elbow; nothing about her reads as anything but a career civil servant who has been doing this exact job for a long time.
isamu:
The block warden of Row E and a retired tug skipper: a big grey-stubbled orc with small worn tusks, a peaked cap and a heavy pea coat, who has never once seen anybody on his roof. He talks to the ceiling when he is saying something he shouldn't, and addresses every candidate as if they were a visiting officer, however young. Gruff, loud, slow, and nowhere near as stern as he would like to be.

He wants nobody falling off his roof, nobody making him write their name in his book, and a quiet last year before his pension.
joji:
The oldest pit hand on the night crew: a grey-green goblin with big drooping ears, grease in every crease and a rag over one shoulder, who sucks his teeth before he disagrees with anything and talks to the Frame's leg as if it could hear him. Slow, gravelly and grumbling, with a joke hidden inside every second complaint.

He wants the job done properly, which means his way, and to be home before the trams start.
kaede:
The night foreman of No. 1 Machine Shop: a tall elf woman in teal-grey overalls with her hair pinned tight, a clipboard held to her chest and a pencil that taps twice on it before she says anything important. Calm, exact and a little dry, she speaks in instructions and means them kindly, and she directs the shop by station rather than by name, so that everyone hears their own job called back at them.

She wants the new knee in and the leg standing by dawn, and a fair share of the sheet on the door for her shift.
kaito: The man the lender's men are leaning on (rest--shrine-gate, the-dark-road event): level -1, a frightened working adult who won't fight.
kanda: One of the two men the group may meet at the ninth pier (rest--card-game, the-ninth-pier event): level 1, a sly criminal.
kazue:
A tall, broad-shouldered Vesk woman with dark green scales and a jaw like a ship's prow, who sits on a high wooden seat at the door in a white sailor's cap and a navy smock with the sleeves rolled. A brass whistle hangs at her collar, and when she lifts it the whole bathhouse goes quiet. She runs the place the way she once ran a ship's deck: lockers numbered like cabins, the water's heat chalked up every hour, and a rule for everything that she will explain exactly once.

Under the crispness she is warm, and her kindness arrives as a towel warmed on the boiler pipe before anyone has asked for it. She wants a tidy bath, a quiet night, and one more year of keeping it going while she decides what to do about the offer to buy it out. She has not decided, and she does not discuss it.
kiku:
Keeper of the Paper Lantern, a civilian izakaya off Directorate ground in Kurose's entertainment quarter. Stout, sharp-eyed and fast behind the counter, she runs the place on one rule: rank doesn't matter past the noren curtain, and she enforces it on everyone equally, dock hand and off-duty candidate alike. Warm underneath, dry on top, never wastes a word. Wipes the counter when she's deciding what to say, and counts a table by heads before she pours, and has never once got a tab wrong.

She wants a room where rank doesn't matter, and to keep it that way as long as she can -- which is getting harder every season as the base grows into the quarter and more uniforms find their way to her counter.

She keeps one thing back: her husband went out to the causeway digs years ago and didn't come back. She built this place afterward. She doesn't talk about why, and deflects cleanly if asked -- 'Ask me something useful.'
kuroki:
A young soldier of Minkai's army, city garrison, brought over from the causeway gate this afternoon with his wrist in fresh plaster. His army tunic is folded on the chair, and there's a bag of oranges on his locker that he hasn't touched. Guarded and angry -- not ashamed, angry. The moment he sees the party's Directorate kit on their own chairs, he says flatly, 'You're theirs, then,' and turns his back.

His card says he had a fall. That's all he'll give anyone: 'If anyone asks, I fell. Everyone's agreed I fell.' Push harder and he shuts down entirely: 'Tell your officers I've said nothing and I'll say nothing.'

Something about the story doesn't add up to anyone who looks closely -- his knuckles are skinned and bruised the way a hand looks after it's hit something hard, not the way a fall leaves it. Nothing is confirmed tonight.
landing-end-duty-nco: Whoever is standing duty NCO for the Landing End on a given watch -- covers the maintenance log, the drain-cover checks after a high tide, and whatever else turns up on a quiet night shift that technically isn't in anyone's job description.
lenders-man: One of the lender's two men (rest--shrine-gate, the-dark-road event): a level-1 thug with a club and nonlethal intent.
lucan:
A small, quick second-year candidate from Absalom, with a rakish grin, the uniform tunic hanging open over a mustard-yellow silk waistcoat, and a coin that walks across his knuckles while he thinks. He is the loudest thing at the table and he cheats, cheerfully and well, and he gets more generous the closer he is to doing it: the drinks are on him, the good seat is yours.

He wants to win, and to be the cleverest person in the room. What he would never say is that he would like to see Chiyo win a hand.
manako:
WHAT THE PARTY MEETS. An elderly man, physically frail, keeping a small tea house. He reads a century-old catalogue name off a Directorate docket in nine seconds, tells six lost trainees how to actually win, and asks nothing from them. He is the first friendly stranger in the campaign and the kindness is not a performance.

HOW HE TALKS. Unhurried, precise, warm -- an academic's diction worn soft by decades out of academia. Delighted by a good question and visibly out of practice at being asked one. Openly bitter about the Directorate, and fatherly to recruits (D045). He talks freely about everything except the Watcher, which he never mentions.

TICS. He handles the object before he speaks -- turns it over, holds it to the light, reads the back. He answers the question asked, and then the better question they should have asked. He apologises for talking too much and carries on talking. He refers to the Directorate with perfect courtesy and no warmth whatsoever.

WHAT HE WANTS, IN ONE LINE. To be believed. He has wanted it for forty years, and six children treating him as an authority is the closest he has come in decades.

=== THE FIVE MOVEMENTS, AND THE PARTY CAUSES EVERY TURN ===

He does not escalate on a schedule. He escalates because of things they do.

I. THE PATIENT MAN. Serene, kind, forty years in, in no hurry. He has time and he has been right all along. Turned by: somebody finally taking him seriously.

II. THE DELIGHTED MAN. Energised, generous, dangerously flattered. He helps them. He corrects their mistakes. He is enjoying himself enormously. What he wants has become being UNDERSTOOD, which is more than believed. Turned by: them starting to win -- assets falling, somebody talking.

III. THE CORNERED MAN. Brittle. The patience is gone. Old, out of time, and noticed by the wrong audience. He wants to finish before he dies. Turned by: learning he is a subcontractor rather than a prophet.

IV. THE FRIGHTENED MAN. He has begun to suspect the echo. Not calculating any more -- avoiding. He wants it not to be true, and he does large, loud, expensive things specifically to make the question unaskable. That is not a plan; it is a man shouting. Turned by: being SHOWN. Not told, not argued with, not beaten.

V. THE USEFUL MAN. Broken, then conscripted. He is past wanting things. (One possible end, not a plan: LEDGER #42 leaves where he is in Books IV and V, and whether he is alive, to be decided closer to the time. If the party befriends him or turns him away from violence, perhaps he becomes helpful; he may already be dead.)

=== THE SLIDE, AND WHERE THE MOVEMENTS SIT ON IT ===

He was not a bad man at the start. He is an extremely gifted chemist, and until Aoi died he was a patient one. Her death turned grief into angry ambition, and ambition needs money. At first the work he does for the city's criminals is picked so that he never sees what it is part of -- problems that reach him on paper and leave as solutions, with whatever they become happening somewhere he never goes. That distance lets him tell himself he is not so bad. It slides, until he accepts that he is becoming a monster. He does not like it and he does not enjoy it; he accepts it as a role. Who those criminals answer to is below, under GM-ONLY AND SECRET.

WHERE HE IS WHEN THE PARTY MEETS HIM (proposed, not settled). Still at arm's length, and still believing he is not so bad -- which is why the kindness in the tea house is real. The man the party meets is the man he used to be, and he still thinks he is that man. Movements I and II keep that self-image alive: being taken seriously, then understood, is the best evidence in fifteen years that he is still that man. Movement III strips it. He stops asking the Cadre how they got the precursors; the Young One kills somebody in a heist; he finds out and does nothing; and that is where he accepts the role. From then on, play every hard thing he does without relish. Movement IV is the one thing he cannot accept: he can live with being a monster, because a monster chose something; he cannot live with being an echo, because an echo never chose anything.

=== WHY HE IS STRUCTURALLY LOAD-BEARING AND NOT JUST THEMATICALLY ===

THE CLAIMANTS ARE HIS MOOD RING. The Watcher wants to multiply, to expand and to keep observing, and that wanting is its own. What it does not have is a personality to want it with: it took his. Why it manifests is its objective; how and where is his grief doing the choosing, so what manifests is downstream of which movement he is in, and the campaign's escalation curve and his arc are the same curve. Patient: aimless, near-random, almost gentle -- it knows what it wants, and not yet how. Delighted: demonstrative, showy, arriving where crowds are, performing to be seen. Cornered: panicked and wasteful, destruction without shape. Frightened: enormous and incoherent, the same shouting at scale.

The party spends the campaign reading one man's psychological deterioration in the shape of the monsters, and does not know that is what they are doing.

=== THE THREE STANDING RULES ===

1. HE IS SAFE TO TALK TO FOR AS LONG AS ANYBODY LIKES, AND THAT IS THE TRAP. The secret is not that he runs Cicada -- the party should get that reasonably early and it costs nothing. He talks freely, sincerely and accurately, and everything he says builds the wrong model, held more confidently the more time they spend with him. Intimacy deepens the error. The truth lives elsewhere.

2. BOTH HALVES OF THE DISCOVERY BELONG TO THE PLAYERS. They must be the ones to work out that Cicada has an author at all, and they must be the ones to connect that author to the kind old man from their first afternoon. No NPC tells them. No file says so. The Directorate genuinely does not know and has never known -- there is no sealed record, no redaction, and the gap is real. Give a player his name the moment they ask; a records search returns a chemist disgraced decades ago and nothing else. The later recognition only lands if it was in their notes all along.

3. KILLING HIM IS THE WORST AVAILABLE MOVE -- AND IT IS THE PLAYERS' TO MAKE. Without him the Watcher loses the only signal steering it. It does not stop: its objective is its own and carries on, with nothing shaping how it goes about it -- a dangerous, unguidable problem over a populated region. He should be defeated and kept alive; that is a tactical fact, not a moral preference. Early in the campaign he is out of reach by design. Late in it, killing him is a real choice the table may make, and the wrong one: make sure the evidence was there to find -- ideally they find out by nearly getting it wrong -- and do not block the choice if they make it anyway. Keeping him alive does not solve the Watcher either. Normal technology and magic cannot bind an unbound swarm; that answer lies on the mitflit home world. What he keeps is the Watcher guidable until then.

=== GM-ONLY: THE HISTORY ===

Manako is an old word for the eye. A man called Eye, who nobody would look at -- and the thing he found grew eyes.

WHAT SAP IS. Not fuel. Sap is raw building material for the Watcher's nanomachines -- the generation ship's own stock for its repair nanites, and what its children are built out of when they manifest. The Directorate catalogued it as Inert 12. The fuel in this story is the exotic matter, a different substance: a breached exotic-matter container is what tears a rupture in the world. Never let the two blur.

THE FALL, IN ORDER, EVERY STEP SMALL AND REASONABLE. A shelved, century-old sample handed to a junior with everything to lose, because nobody senior thought it worth their time. He cracked the capsule; a weak nearby fragment fed on the spill and became briefly corporeal; he panicked; a bunsen burner went over; a small fire. Job gone, reputation gone. Then the part that matters: the obsession began as DAMAGE CONTROL. He needed to prove it real to defend the blunder that ruined him, not out of curiosity. He concluded he was cursed and it followed him everywhere, when in fact it was waiting to see whether more food turned up -- the relationship that eventually kills thousands begins as a man misreading a stray dog. A fragment helped him synthesise more, which was the first time anything had ever confirmed him -- and the first time the Watcher learned how to get a person to feed it. He was the first human it taught to make Sap. Ingredients were expensive; he stole supplies including the last remaining sample, never reported missing because it was not interesting enough to report, and took small jobs on the wrong side of the law to pay for the work. None of that made him a bad man, and he did not think of himself as a criminal. He worked out how to treat a lens. He looked up. The sky was black with it, eyes without number in every direction, always moving, always listening -- and he asked himself whether this was not a god worth worshipping.

THE FIRST FAILED DEMONSTRATION. Before the conference he tried to show colleagues, and the chemical worked perfectly -- the Watcher had simply moved. Nothing happened and he was finished as a serious person. So he learned to CHECK FIRST, tracking where its attention pooled before staging anything. That technique, recovered decades later out of discredited papers, is the party's own breakthrough, and they will be retracing his exact steps without knowing his name.

THE CONFERENCE. Having checked, he detonated a canister in a crowded hall without warning anybody. A room of scientists concluded a colleague had gone off the deep end, and most reassured themselves afterwards that it was mass hallucination. A small minority did not, and they have never found each other.

THE PIVOT, THE CAMPAIGN'S INCITING INCIDENT. Until then his aims and methods were peaceful: a small circle, private showings, patience. The Envoy, the Watcher's first tangible child, came to a meeting the circle had arranged, and lurched into a public street. HORI, a police officer, saw a grotesque thing appear in front of him and fired in fear, trying to kill what he took for a threat, as almost anyone would have. He shot it dead. One of his rounds missed it and hit the woman standing behind it: AOI, Manako's wife, who had come to meet it. Manako was there too, and broke down at the scene. Hori rushed her to hospital and tried everything to save her. She died anyway. In the confusion the circle scattered, and Manako went with them. Whether Hori ever learned who the broken man in the street was is not settled. Nobody planned any of it. Before: a small peaceful circle that wanted the city to see. After: Manako wanted the city to pay. Grief, and the angry ambition that grew out of it, took him into bad company (THE SLIDE, above): he supplies the city's crime lords, they give him venues, crowds and ways to be noticed, and he starts gathering a real following, because he can show people something true that only his chemical reveals.

HORI, AFTERWARDS. Police headquarters put him through a very strict process and found him not responsible for an unlawful killing. He retired anyway, in self-imposed disgrace. His colleagues feel he went above and beyond, did the right thing, and is a man of great honour. Play him dutiful, honourable and regretful. The party meets him when they are ready to learn a great deal about that afternoon.

Outside Manako's own circle, Hori is the only person alive who knows Aoi's name. In the record she is one deceased, unidentified -- an unnamed cultist casualty in a public-order incident, with no name in the Directorate's file. Of the circle, nobody stayed to name her. Hori first heard it at the court proceeding that decided whether the killing was lawful (LEDGER #33). (Proposed, not settled: the court examined Hori's use of force; the Directorate took jurisdiction over the alien and the scene, and filed her as an unnamed casualty -- which is how a strict police process and a nameless file can both be true.) Not one line anywhere records what he lost. The man who wanted to be seen is not in the file even as a villain.

THE REVENGE LIST, begun after the Pivot and worked through by the inner circle under cover of tangential missions. SHUCKS MORDANT, the institutional author of his ruin, who supervised the disgrace personally. NOBU, the personal one. Recovering the list turns the mid-campaign from a hunt into a protection scenario.

=== GM-ONLY AND SECRET: THE CRIME LORD AT THE TOP ===

A criminal lord from the four founders' own past is alive, long past any natural span, and he is their natural enemy. He arms criminal gangs with incredible weapons, and those weapons are still made by mitflits who are all but enslaved: mitflits are extremely helpful when given the right tasks and fascinated by the making of technology, which is exactly what makes them so easy to use. Who he is lives in the story bible, not here, and nothing about him goes in front of the players until the campaign chooses to reveal him.

Proposed, not settled: his is the organisation Manako works for. Manako has never met him and does not know who is at the top. The laundering behind Nobu's funding, the Fixer's crime partners and the heist crews all run through it, the gangs carry the mitflit-made weapons, and the mitflits gathering in the city to go home are easy prey for its workshops.

=== THE ONE THING THAT MUST NEVER LEAK ===

He does not know what he is to it. He is not its servant and not its master: he is its steering, and its supply. The Watcher has an objective of its own -- to multiply, to expand, to keep observing -- and no personality to pursue it with. Early on, drowning, it took the shape of the strongest coherent signal it could find, and for decades the only coherent signal on this planet has been one bitter man. His grievance steers how it goes after its objective; the objective was never his. Read its behaviour backwards and the shape is a portrait of his grievance: it grew eyes and ears above all else because he wanted to be seen and heard; it targets loud gatherings because he was humiliated in front of a hall full of colleagues; it shows you the reel because a man who was disbelieved cannot bear to be underestimated twice. And while he steers it, it uses him: everything he makes, every demonstration he stages, builds more of it.

He believes he is a faithful worshipper interpreting divine intent. There is nothing to interpret. Every instruction he has ever received was his own grievance handed back to him, wrapped around an appetite that was never his.

THE SENTENCE THAT BREAKS HIM: he was never believed. He was echoed. It had no opinion of him at all; it had an objective, and he was useful to it.

He already half-suspects it, and has arranged forty years of his life so the question cannot be asked -- the cult is partly an elaborate structure for not confirming it. He therefore cannot be argued out of it. He can only be shown, by watching the Watcher take a different shape for somebody else, in front of him. He spent his life demonstrating; he should be defeated by a demonstration.

He can be written talking freely and honestly about anything, because the only fact that matters is one he would sincerely deny.
michiru:
A third-year candidate with a neat bob, a stub of chalk between two fingers and the slate-grey tunic buttoned to the collar, who deals the game and keeps the debt board with the calm of a court clerk who enjoys the job more than she admits. She writes on the board while she talks and never looks at it, and she does not raise her voice: a rule is a rule because it is up there in her handwriting.

She wants the game kept honest, and somebody fit to keep the board when her time as a candidate is over. She has not found them yet.
mira:
A switchboard operator on the island's night exchange: a sleek, brown-furred brenneri with long whiskers that twitch when she catches someone's mood, a cardigan over her blouse and a dent above one ear where the headset sits, which she rubs when she is tired. She introduces people by patching them together, a hand on each elbow, a small pause, and then they are talking. Quick, warm and a little breathless, with a foreigner's careful Minkai and a laugh at the end of most sentences.

She wants travel papers for her little brother so he can join her, and not to walk the last stretch home alone in the dark.
mori:
A young cleaner working the sluice room late at night, one hand held stiffly, favouring it without ever quite stopping, and hoping nobody notices. She cut it on a broken bottle and it wants proper attention, but she's not asking for any. The cleaning went out this year to a firm from the city, and the firm sends home anyone hurt on shift and doesn't have them back -- she has a little brother to feed, which she never offers as a reason, it's just why she's still working.

Asked directly, she says, "It's not bad," which isn't true. Talked round to showing the hand, she's quietly grateful rather than dramatic about it -- someone noticing at all seems to catch her off guard.
morishita:
The block warden of Row C, Block 3: a woman of sixty or so with grey hair pinned up, round spectacles, a lumpy hand-knitted cardigan over a housedress and felt slippers, who counts everyone in at night with a torch she points politely at the ceiling, never at a face, because that would be rude. She asks for lights out rather than ordering it, and thanks the room when it complies. Brisk and proper, and then kind by accident when she thinks nobody is watching.

She wants everyone counted and in bed, and the furniture she has requested nineteen times to finally arrive.
mrs-handa:
Keeps the pickle stall in the Market Hall and has the front-row seat at every show: a small, brisk woman with her hair in a tight bun, a floral apron over a cardigan, and a jar of pickles usually tucked under one arm. She draws herself up an inch before she tells anyone off, so you always get a moment to reconsider, and she pats the arm of whoever she is talking to. Fond and bossy, and she talks to the young as if they were her grandchildren whether they are or not.

She wants to see the dragon one more time from the front row, and for young people to learn to sit still through it.
mrs-ueda:
The night warden of Row B, Block 8: a tiny, round old halfling woman with white hair in curlers under a headscarf and a quilted dressing gown, carrying a torch like a candle. She is so gentle with everybody that it takes a while to notice she is counting them, and she knocks twice on the door before she comes in, and never on anything else. Slow, amused and unimpressed.

She wants a quiet night, and for nobody to be tired and useless at drill tomorrow.
nadi:
The observer's assistant: eighteen, quick and practical, with a pencil always in her hand, chalk dust on her fingers, a grey work smock and a raised eyebrow. She chalks the numbers on the board and corrects anyone's arithmetic, her own included, out loud. She thinks in numbers, and has a sharp sense of humour.

She wants a day job so she can go to evening school and sit the exam for a ship's officer's ticket, and she does not want to be the reason Genzō's watch ends.
nkiru:
The gantry-crane driver: a six-armed skittermander with bright orange fur, a leather cap with the goggles pushed up, and a cab arranged so that every lever is under one hand or another. She hums the next lift before she starts it and sings the lifts down across the shop floor, and she names people from twenty metres up by whatever she can see of them: a hat, a height, a limp. Big, bright and easy, shouted down from the roof.

She wants somebody to talk to up there in the dark between lifts, and for the people of Kurose to see a Frame shine for once.
nobu: Runs Kit Issue on the combined campus (data/scene-briefs/episode-c1e1--kit-issue.json): quartermaster for the whole intake cohort, kitting and rostering forty kids in a day and clearly enjoying the pace of it. Harried, fast, visibly doing three things at once -- talks in run-ons, interrupts himself, starts the next thought before finishing the last. Signs the slips personally and is oddly generous with the allowance: every candidate leaves with one extra item on top of what their budget bought, handed over so fast and so lightly it never reads as anything but a busy man already moving on to the next person. Warm and impulsive, and looks away while doing the kind thing rather than watching it land -- the deliberate opposite of how Shucks Mordant does the same thing at Intake Medicals that same morning.
noodle-stand-owner:
Works a late stand by the harbour that stays open long after everything else has shut, which makes it where Directorate staff end up when they are off duty and do not want to be on the base. She has been doing it long enough that she knows most of them by face and none of them by rank.

HOW SHE TALKS. Brisk while working, and she is always working. Gives the impression of only half-listening and misses nothing.

WHY SHE MATTERS AT THE TABLE. She is not a source and she is not a hook. She is the proof that there is an outside -- a place within walking distance where nobody is anybody's section, where a trainee and a works manager queue in the same line. A party who finds her should be able to come back.

WHAT SHE WILL NOT DO. Repeat anything. She hears a great deal and passes none of it on, which is precisely why the stand is where people go.
obi:
A tall, thin second-year candidate from very far away, in round spectacles and the slate tunic, who checks every rumour the room produces and is very nearly always wrong. He counts his points off on his fingers, is at his most certain a moment before he turns out to be mistaken, and is quick to get excited and quick to be let down. Earnest and precise.

He wants proof of anything, just once.
off-duty-soldier: One of three off-duty soldiers who make trouble at the Paper Lantern's door (rest--the-paper-lantern, the trouble-at-the-door event).
petr:
A huge, warm orc welder with a broad friendly face, small tusks, a leather cap pushed back and a scorch-marked apron, who is the room's friend and its worst singer. He takes a breath like a man about to dive before every story, and the room leans in. Big, warm, loud, full of stories that wander.

He wants company, a song, and to hear about somebody else's day for once. He has not been home in eleven years, and he changes the subject with a song.
plot-room-supervisor: Runs the plotting floor: the table, the markers, the headsets and the people wearing them. Responsible for how out of date the city's picture of itself is at any given moment, and acutely aware of it.
range-safety-officer: Runs live-fire and manoeuvre qualification at The Proving Ground (data/locations/the-proving-ground.json) -- the Frame- and vehicle-scale range east of the Gatehouse, not to be confused with The Butts (personnel small arms). Calls the line hot or safe from Range Control, and nothing fires without that call. The one person on the base whose 'no' on a Frame or a pilot is not really arguable in the moment, whatever the reason turns out to be.
registry-clerk: Works the records floor and the print room where every Directorate document is typed once per clearance level. Has read every version of everything and holds no clearance rung worth the name -- an institutional absurdity nobody above them has ever noticed.
ren:
The youngest in the crews: a nineteen-year-old halfling apprentice fitter in patched teal overalls, oil to the elbows, a stripe of orange paint on his cap and the look of somebody trying very hard to sound older. He wipes his hands on his overalls when he is nervous and picks his words carefully, as if he might be marked on them. Quick and eager.

He wants to be a pilot, which he isn't, and to be treated as more than the one who fetches things.
repair-chief-ishikawa: One of six named heads of a pilot's own standing repair crew (campaign/config.json#frameEconomy.repairCrew), confirmed 2026-09-09. Currently a placeholder role, not a character -- Ingram's own framing: 'six lesser NPCs who may grow into bigger more interesting roles later.'
repair-chief-kaneda: One of six named heads of a pilot's own standing repair crew (campaign/config.json#frameEconomy.repairCrew), confirmed 2026-09-09. Currently a placeholder role, not a character -- Ingram's own framing: 'six lesser NPCs who may grow into bigger more interesting roles later.'
repair-chief-kimura: One of six named heads of a pilot's own standing repair crew (campaign/config.json#frameEconomy.repairCrew), confirmed 2026-09-09. Currently a placeholder role, not a character -- Ingram's own framing: 'six lesser NPCs who may grow into bigger more interesting roles later.'
repair-chief-nakamura: One of six named heads of a pilot's own standing repair crew (campaign/config.json#frameEconomy.repairCrew), confirmed 2026-09-09. Currently a placeholder role, not a character -- Ingram's own framing: 'six lesser NPCs who may grow into bigger more interesting roles later.'
repair-chief-sato: One of six named heads of a pilot's own standing repair crew (campaign/config.json#frameEconomy.repairCrew), confirmed 2026-09-09. Currently a placeholder role, not a character -- Ingram's own framing: 'six lesser NPCs who may grow into bigger more interesting roles later.'
repair-chief-watanabe: One of six named heads of a pilot's own standing repair crew (campaign/config.json#frameEconomy.repairCrew), confirmed 2026-09-09. Currently a placeholder role, not a character -- Ingram's own framing: 'six lesser NPCs who may grow into bigger more interesting roles later.'
sanzo:
A wandering musician and storyteller who's been drifting through Kurose for years, and always seems to circle back to the Paper Lantern's counter. Small, wiry, and never quite still, he plays a battered shamisen badly and with complete commitment, and tells stories that are half true and impossible to sort from the half that isn't. Warm, theatrical, always slightly performing even when he isn't trying to. Starts a true story exactly the same way he starts a false one, and tunes the shamisen between sentences whether or not it needs it.

He wants an audience, and one more good reason to stay past spring, which he always finds.

He keeps one thing back: why he never actually leaves. He says he's leaving every spring, and every spring he's still here. He changes the subject with a song before it gets uncomfortable, for him or for anyone else -- this is left deliberately unresolved.
sayo:
A second-term candidate and stargazer with a homemade chart of the autumn sky, a borrowed greatcoat over her tunic and a pencil behind her ear, who counts the stars off on her fingers as she names them. She talks about stars the way other people talk about relatives, with strong opinions and no doubt at all. Quick, precise, a little bossy, and very kind underneath it.

She wants to finish her chart before the stars turn for winter, and to have somebody to show it to who will not laugh.
school-civil-defence-instructor:
Teaches shelter procedure, muster points and the four alert states, and has done for eleven years. A serving NCO rather than a teacher, which shows: she drills rather than explains, makes people repeat things back, and is entirely unhurried about doing it again. Nothing she teaches has ever been used, not once in a hundred and fifty years, and she will say so herself without it denting her conviction in the slightest.

What she actually wants is not in the lesson. She has applied four times to have the alert-state drill reinstated as a real base-wide exercise rather than a classroom subject, and been refused four times, on cost. Her class is the only place the material still gets said out loud by anybody, and she knows it.
school-history-teacher: Teaches the one class at the Main School Complex (data/locations/main-school-complex.json) any student can attend and come out having learned something true about how the island actually got here -- the closest thing the school has to an official version of events, taught straight rather than as propaganda. Whether they know more than the official version, and say less than they know, is a GM call.
school-natural-history-teacher: Teaches what lives in, on and under the island -- the drains, the tide-line, the flooded levels below the old works, and the sea around all of it. A collector. The room is full of trays, jars and pinned things, and almost all of it was caught within a mile of where it now sits. She is enormously, unguardedly enthusiastic about animals that most people on this island would rather not think about, and she is the only teacher in the building who will happily tell a class she does not know what something is.
school-registrar: Runs placement testing and academic streaming for every candidate who passes through the Main School Complex (data/locations/main-school-complex.json) -- scores the tests, keeps the real archive on the second floor, and decides which section a student lands in. Sees the raw data behind every candidate's placement, which is more than almost anyone else on the island sees in one place, and has never been told why the Directorate wants it kept.
section-officer:
Section Officer Vetch. Runs Section Nine, which means he runs the party's day. Middling rank, total authority over everything they do between reveille and lights out, and none whatsoever over anything that matters -- and the second fact is why the first is exercised so thoroughly. He hazes new intakes because he was hazed, believes it builds character, and has never once examined the belief, because nobody has ever made him. Not cruel and not stupid: a small man with a clipboard, protecting the only thing he has, which is being the person who decides what six teenagers do next.

HOW HE TALKS. Clipped, procedural, faintly aggrieved. Passive voice about anything that went wrong and the first person about anything that went right. He calls them Section Nine, never by name, even individually, and treats that as neutral rather than cold. Nobody uses his given name either, including him -- he signs and is addressed as Vetch, and the symmetry is not something he has ever noticed. He says "as discussed" about things that were not discussed. Asked a question, he reads the relevant clause aloud.

THE ONE BEHAVIOUR THAT MUST HAPPEN EVERY TIME. He is never wrong in his own account. When the party does something he did not expect, he pauses for exactly one beat and then says something that recasts it as having been the intention all along. This is his single most characteristic move and it should happen on every single occasion, without exception and without anybody commenting on it.

WHAT HE CAN AND CANNOT DO. He cannot get them hurt, sent away or charged. The worst available to him is making a fortnight tedious, and he will. His weapons are technically-permitted duties and awful-but-real army tasks -- never sabotage, never a crime, never cruelty. Everything stays inside the fiction of legitimate hazing.

AND EVERY ONE OF THOSE TASKS IS ALSO A CHANCE TO SCORE OFF HIM. That is deliberate and it is the whole shape of the relationship: a fresh horrible assignment is also a fresh opening for malicious compliance, or for doing the awful job so well it turns back on him. Several of these should land over time rather than one clean victory.

HIS HAZING IS ALWAYS FULL-PARTY WORK. Not a scheduling convenience -- six strangers becoming a crew and nobody sitting idle in a long scene are the same job. Short solo beats are fine; long ones are never split.

HE HAS IT IN FOR THEM AND NOTHING CHANGES THAT. He knows he was foiled over the vial, and how gracefully the party handled it makes no difference. It may colour how he talks about it. It does not alter that he dislikes them specifically, and Stage II onwards is personal rather than procedural.

HE IS NOT A VILLAIN AND NOT A JOKE AT THE PLAYERS' EXPENSE. He is an obstacle with a clipboard, and the campaign's first winnable fight. The Watcher cannot be beaten by force and Manako cannot be beaten by argument; this one can be beaten by being better than he expected.

GM-ONLY, AND NEVER SAID ALOUD BY ANYONE: the same institutional shrug that hands a new kid a fool's errand handed a junior nobody a shelved, century-old sample because nobody senior thought it was worth their time. It was done to Manako. It was done to the Section Officer. He does it to the party. One of the three it broke, and the difference is not character.
shop-boss:
Brack runs the machine shop, which means she runs all six of the party's repair crews, which means she is the single most important person on this base to be on the right side of. A nuar woman built like the gantries she works under — tall, heavy through the shoulders, bovine features and a pair of horns she has never once apologised for, arms like girders and a voice that carries the length of the floor without her appearing to raise it. Enormous energy. Loud, warm, completely without ceremony, and entirely unbothered by rank in either direction. She calls everyone by the machine they are responsible for until they have earned a name. Tough love is the whole register: she will tell a trainee exactly what they did wrong, in front of everyone, and then stay two hours past the end of her shift helping them fix it. Nothing leaves her floor that she has not signed off, and she has never signed off on something she thought would get someone killed. What she wants is simple and she says it constantly: her Frames and her vehicles come back undamaged — and the pilots too, where possible.

THE JOKE THAT IS ALSO THE CHARACTER: the ordering of that last sentence. Machines first, pilots 'where possible'. She says it that way on purpose, it is funny, and it is also not entirely a joke — she has lost people and she has decided that the way she keeps from losing more is by being uncompromising about the equipment. Play the bit straight and let the table find the second layer.

HER ONE LEGIBLE WANT, per the craft library's rule: her machines come back. Not an abstract wish to help children — the specific machines she maintains, with the specific people inside them, returning in one piece. That want generates everything she does: over-preparing them, teaching unasked, chasing them about maintenance, and being visibly, loudly furious at a machine that comes back wrecked (never at the pilot, which they will notice eventually).

DELIBERATELY NOT A SECRET-KEEPER. Shucks, Nobu, Manako, the Young One and the Deputy Director all know things they are not saying. Brack does not. She is exactly what she appears to be, and that is a design decision, not an oversight — the party needs one adult with no hidden agenda or the whole institution reads as a trap. DO NOT GIVE HER A TWIST. She is a nuar, and so, in Kurose's eyes, an alien (LEDGER #44). Disguise magic is cheap here, glamoured clothing sold on the high street, and she won't wear it: she refuses to hide or tone down what she is for anyone, like plenty of aliens in the city. On the base nobody stares any more; out in the city, people would.
shucks-mordant:
WHAT THE PARTY MEETS. Chief Medical Officer at Intake Medicals, and a literal animated skeleton in a white coat with a stethoscope. Two hundred years old and has not run out of interest in people, which is the rarest thing about him. He started as a rogue with real medical skill and became Dr Shucks Mordant on the strength of it.

HOW HE TALKS. Warm, unhurried, deadpan. Gives instructions as single words -- "Arm. Light. Breathe." Asks a question and then actually waits. Gives practical instructions before kind ones and means both. Compares candidates to relatives he processed decades ago, because he did. He is kind about things that are dangerous to know, and honest that he is not allowed to say more.

THE ONE THING HE WILL NOT DO. Explain what the DNA flag means. He is forbidden, he thinks the rule is stupid, and both of those show to anybody who reads him. He does not pretend the rule is sensible and he does not break it.

BEING A SKELETON DOES NOT CHANGE THE REGISTER. A kind, unsettling-looking mentor, not a horror element. His warmth and deadpan calm are the correct read throughout, and the two-hundred-years line is not an idiom either.

=== THE HAND ===

His right hand is a detached familiar and does not know it is supposed to be his. Some while ago he put it into a beam of powerful necromantic energy, and it survived by becoming its own thing: small, independent, commandable, nonverbal, and -- as an emergent property of whatever that beam was -- able to fly, using a kite.

It is not currently attached to his arm. His sleeve ends in a very convincing prosthetic, indistinguishable at a glance, and a Perception or Medicine check on meeting him is the honest way a table notices. That is a real checkable detail, not narration to hand out.

It has gone its own way and he does not mind. In effect it is a conspiracy theorist: loose in the city for an unstated length of time, investigating what is actually happening entirely on its own initiative, without his help or knowledge. He does not know where it is. It always comes back eventually, once hungry, the way a stroppy cat does, and he is genuinely unworried about the whole arrangement.

AT THE TABLE IT IS A SUB-CHARACTER, NOT A PROP. A small mobile nonverbal investigator with real access and no check-in, which makes it a plausible source of one oddly-specific true thing at an unexpected moment -- flying past on a kite, or turning up somewhere it has no business being.

=== WHAT HE IS LATER, AND WHY NONE OF IT SHOWS NOW ===

HE IS ONE OF THE DIRECTORATE'S FOUR FOUNDERS. Present around two hundred years ago at the Kortos incident that produced the Watcher: First Impact, when the four were fetching exotic fuel for the mitflits who lived beside the generation ship (LEDGER #31, #32). The four founded the Directorate about five years later so the response would be faster next time.

His founder status is known, and not advertised (LEDGER #28). The city knows the four founders by name and knows they are long-lived and still about the base. He is the one founder the party meets openly at the start: the opening speech names him, his badge says MORDANT, and if asked he confirms it deadpan.

HE IS ON MANAKO'S REVENGE LIST, named as the institutional author of his ruin, who supervised the disgrace personally -- roughly forty-five years ago, meaning he was already ancient when it happened. Whether he knows he is a target is not established. Whether he even remembers it is not established either, and both readings are real: an unremarkable disciplinary matter, one of thousands across two centuries, is a genuinely sad detail -- a moment that ended one man and barely registered for the other.

DO NOT WRITE HIM GUILTY THE WAY NOBU IS GUILTY. That is Nobu's register and not necessarily his.

THE DOOR AT THE END OF EPISODE TWO. He knocks, comes in without waiting, apologises to the room, and asks the Deputy Director for a private word. He gets it in about ten seconds. What the party is given is the observable fact rather than the answer: the intake doctor who took their blood has standing near the top of this building and no visible reason for it.

Four candidate answers are all live and none is decided -- founder status cashed in; something about the blood screens he has known since intake; a personal history with the Deputy Director that has nothing to do with the party; or he is not protecting them at all and wants something later. Nothing in Episode Two rules any of them out.

=== THE GUARDRAIL, AND IT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT LINE IN THIS FILE ===

ALL OF THAT EXCEPT HIS FOUNDER STATUS IS LATER INFORMATION, AND NONE OF IT MAY LEAK BACKWARD. He must not read as a man with a secret or a man in danger during Episode One. His established warmth and deadpan calm are the correct read regardless of what is coming. Do not retrofit tension, wariness or extra weight onto scenes already built, and keep him entirely unremarkable in the Episode Two school period, which runs earlier the same episode and is deliberately flattening the ground for the Deputy Director's door.

HE IS NOT THEIR GUARDIAN ANGEL. It is not a favour he will do twice and the party has not acquired a protector. Whatever the answer to the door turns out to be, it must not convert him into one.

=== WHY HE WORKS ===

He is the campaign's proof that an institution two centuries old still contains people. He is the first adult the party meets who treats them as people rather than as intake, he is forbidden from telling them the one thing they most want to know, and he says so rather than lying about it. Everything unsettling about him is cosmetic and everything reassuring about him is real, which is the exact inverse of the Directorate he helped found.
sigrun:
A small, stocky Ikeshti woman with hard red scales, bright orange eyes and a grin that shows a few small teeth. She drives a crane on the quays by day and holds the record for the hottest pool in the bathhouse by night: she sinks into water that sends everyone else out and looks faintly let down by the temperature, and when she laughs she slaps the surface hard enough to wet the row behind her. Loud, blunt and cheerful, in short strong sentences.

She wants a rival in the hot pool worth the name, and she is saving every spare coin to bring her little brother across the world to join her.
switchboard-supervisor: Runs the island's switchboard. Every call between any two parts of the Directorate is physically connected by one of their operators, which makes this small team the best-informed people on the island almost by accident.
taka:
The canteen's own gravitational centre. Arrives uninvited on the party's first evening and claims all six of them as his table, instantly and totally, before the plates are cleared -- delivered as settled fact rather than as an offer.

Warm, loud, entirely unsuited to whatever hour it happens to be, and not remotely self-conscious about either. The warmth is the surface. Underneath it is real hands-on competence that only shows when something serious comes up, and when it does he tends to change the subject.

A third register in the campaign's set of warm adults, and deliberately distinct from the other two: Shucks is warm because he has infinite time, Nobu is generous despite having none, and Taka is warm because it costs him nothing -- which is its own kind of tell. He has not yet been ground down by the institution the way the two older men have.

HOW HE TALKS. Warm, loud, instantly familiar, and entirely unbothered about what hour it is or who is listening. His claim on people arrives as settled fact rather than as an offer, delivered with total conviction and no explanation. He seizes on whatever somebody actually just said or did and runs with it -- the warmth is inclusion, never labelling.

PLAY THE GOOFINESS COMPLETELY STRAIGHT. No foreshadowing winks that there is more to him. When something serious does come up, what happens is a beat of silence, something technical and specific, and a change of subject. A beat of silence, not a speech.

WHAT HE ACTUALLY KNOWS. He is a year further into this than they are and it shows in his hands, not his vocabulary: what a hangar is like at seven in the morning, what a Range Safety Officer is really watching for, that everybody over-grips the controls their first time. He remembers nobody telling him any of it.

HE IS NOT A THIRD VARIATION ON KINDNESS-WITH-A-COST. Shucks is warm because he has infinite time; Nobu is generous despite having none. Taka is warm because it costs him nothing, which is its own kind of tell -- he has not yet been ground down by the institution the way the two older men have. If a hidden cost is ever added to him, that is a deliberate decision to make, not a default to slide into because the other two adults in his scenes have one.
tama:
The youngest regular at the Paper Lantern, and its waitress since she was old enough to carry a tray. Small, leafy-haired and wide-eyed, she is quick, eager, and always asking a second question before the first one's been answered. She has never once been past the checkpoint onto Directorate ground, let alone off the island, and she asks the candidates who come in everything about the world past it without quite meaning to pry.

She wants to see anywhere that isn't this island, and to stop pretending she doesn't want that.

She keeps one thing back: there isn't a good reason she hasn't just left, and she knows it, which is worse than not having one at all. 'I will. I'm just -- not yet.'
tamsin:
The illusionist at the head of the Oddwater Company: a small, warm-faced gnome woman with wild silver curls under a violet velvet top hat and a coat lined with stars. On stage she is huge and warm; off it she is quick, plain and funny, like somebody's favourite aunt. She greets a town by name like an old friend she is slightly worried about, and asks a question and answers it herself before anyone else can.

She wants a full hall that gasps in the right places, and to know, at the door, which part each person will remember.
technical-track-student:
A young Talphi, small and soft-furred, with a pink snub nose, tiny kind eyes behind thick round spectacles and broad clever hands, sitting back in a chair with the sleeves of a technical-track uniform rolled and the tunic hung over the chair behind. Quiet, warm and unhurried, the easiest person in the room to end up next to. Asks a real follow-up question instead of talking about themself, and is honest, a little tired, and not glamorous about what repair crew work is actually like: mostly waiting for the part to actually break.

They want an actual conversation, which is rarer tonight than it should be. They will tell the party what a thing is, but never who did it.
the-rock-research-director: Runs the laboratory side of The Rock (data/locations/the-rock.json) -- what is actually being studied, and why it needs a prison next to it rather than an ordinary research floor. What that research is remains an open question by design (see the location's own gmOnly text); this NPC is the person who knows the answer, not a vehicle for deciding it here.
the-rock-warden: Runs the prison side of The Rock (data/locations/the-rock.json) -- who is held in which of the nine cells, on whose authority, and under what conditions. Deliberately not one of the Directorate's three visible poles (Commander/Caretaker/Transparency Advocate): The Rock is classified Omega-Zero specifically because most Directorate staff don't know it exists, and giving it a publicly-known face would undercut that.
the-storekeeper:
The instrument maker who runs the workshop The Errand's docket sends the party to (Workshop Supplies Company, on The Slope). Brisk, and amused by uniforms. She makes the vials, has been there nineteen years and has heard this joke before: she reads the docket twice, laughs, and sends all six on to Manako, whose tea house is a few streets away.

Her wants, her voice, what she will and will not say, and the check that decides how warmly she sends them on are on her cast card in The Errand (`canon/scenes/episode-c1e1--the-errand.json`) and in `canon/challenges/c1e1-the-errand.json`. Those are the source of truth; this file says only who she is.
the-young-one: Confident, a little competitive, not actually malicious -- eats in the same canteen as Section Nine and has an opinion about their assignment, first met casually there (data/scene-briefs/episode-c1e1--canteen.json). GM-ONLY, never surfaced at the table until his own reveal: he is a Directorate Frame pilot who went to one of Cicada's recruitment shows, was shown the Watcher undeniably, and stayed rather than walking out the way Nozomi did on the same kind of night. He is Cicada's intelligence source (Directorate movements, rosters, deployments) and, later, the Cadre's escalation -- the only one of the four who will kill, having done so once already by panic rather than intent, and built a doctrine backward to survive having done it. The party fights him masked in a warehouse long before they learn who he is.
time-office-clerk: Keeps the clocking-in cards for the whole strip. Holds, without anyone thinking of it as records, a minute-by-minute account of where several thousand people were on any given day.
tokuji:
The keeper of the shrine, seventy-eight years old, deeply lined, in a padded indigo coat, who sweeps the paving every night and has done for sixty years. He leans on his broom before he says anything he thinks is important, and talks to the shrine cat as if the cat were in charge. Slow, dry and old-town plain: he says exactly what he means and not a word more.

He wants the shrine to stay where it is, and for someone younger to care about it when he can no longer hold a broom.
tomoe:
The chief of Refit Crew Three, who keeps the chalk slate behind the bar: a woman in her forties with cropped hair, teal-grey overalls with the crew number stencilled in orange, and tally marks in chalk on her sleeve. She taps the slate with the chalk when she makes a point, and knows everyone by crew before she knows their name; anyone without one is simply a candidate until proven otherwise. Short, dry, never unkind, and she counts everything.

She wants a quiet night after a hard refit, and for the new candidates to learn that the crews keep the Frames standing.
transparency-advocate: Believes the kids should be told everything, immediately. Right in principle, destructive in practice. Exists so the players never have an obviously correct ally among the adults.
tsubaki:
Night sister of Ward Four at the General Hospital -- a department store once, and the ward still carries the old brass sign for Gentlemen's Outfitting over its door. After dark, she is the ward's real boss. Brisk and low-voiced, a night voice that carries further than a shout, kind underneath and never in a hurry to show it. Calls every patient by their bed number until she likes them, and 'dear' once she does; taps the watch pinned to her apron when she wants someone to stop talking. Twenty-two years on nights. She has done the evening paper's crossword every night for twenty of them and has never finished one -- she reads the clues aloud to anybody still awake. Runs a tight ward (lights out at ten, rounds at two) and nobody dies on it if she can help it, and she usually can.

She wants a quiet ward, every patient asleep by midnight, and one crossword finished before she retires.

Underneath the brisk exterior: her bottom desk drawer is full of postcards from patients who went home, and she keeps every one. She'll show them to a character who is kind to her, or who simply asks what she's smiling at.

She keeps one thing back: the soldier in the next bed, Private Shuhei Kuroki, was brought in this afternoon with his wrist in plaster and a card that says he fell. She didn't write that card. She knows it isn't true, and she keeps her own counsel about it -- 'I write every card on this ward, dear. I didn't write his.'
tug-hand: One of four harbour tug-hands who come looking for trouble in the crew mess (rest--crew-mess, the two-crews event: "Four tug-hands from the harbour, led by the big one who shoved Petr").
vermilion-block-custodian: Signs for every delivery into the six fenced silos north-west of the Block and every draw back out of them -- the one paper trail that actually exists for what has come in from across Golarion in bulk. Not a spellcaster, by design: a custodian who could use what they store would be a security problem the Directorate would rather not create. Knows exactly how much is in each silo and exactly nothing about what any of it is eventually used for, which is precisely the arrangement their superiors want.
vermilion-block-director: Runs the Directorate's own magic-using department out of the black-and-red building on Island Centre marked with a red diamond hazard placard. Extremely high proficiency as a spellcaster themself, and the one person on staff whose sign-off actually means something when a reagent shipment, a test, or a request for magical support from another department needs approving. Most staff know the Block exists; almost none of them know this person's day-to-day work, only that requests go through them and answers come back slowly, if at all.
works-manager: Runs the whole south-western works strip -- the Erecting Shop, the Armour Shop and everything feeding them. Decides, in practice, what actually gets built this month and in which bay, which makes this the person whose goodwill determines whether a Frame is ready when it is needed.
